_meta.scope: U.S. House general-election field for all 38 Texas congressional districts, as printed on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
_meta.method: Every candidate name and party was cross-checked against at least two independent sources: (1) the Texas Tribune's November 2026 sample-ballot dataset, which is built from Texas Secretary of State certification and Associated Press race data; (2) The Green Papers' Texas 2026 General Election page, which tracks the same SOS certification and carries FEC committee IDs; (3) the Wikipedia article '2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas'. All three agree on all 76 major-party nominees. Minor-party and independent ballot qualification was additionally confirmed against the Secretary of State's own independent-candidate filing page. Where sources conflicted, the SOS-derived sources were treated as authoritative and the conflict is recorded in sourcing_flags.
_meta.ballot_names: Names are given in the form used in the SOS/AP ballot data, which is what voters see on the ballot. Fuller legal or alternate name forms appear in the candidate note where they differ.
_meta.incumbent_definition: incumbent: true means the candidate currently serves in the U.S. House representing the district they are running in. A sitting member running in a renumbered or redrawn district they do not currently represent is marked false, with the situation explained in the note. Candidates who previously served in Congress but do not now are not incumbents.
_meta.write_ins: Certified write-in candidates are not printed on the ballot and are therefore not listed under candidates; where Texas certified one for a district, it is stated in that district's race_note.
_meta.neutrality: race_note entries are limited to verifiable structural facts about the race (retirement, vacancy, redistricting change, who is on the ballot). They are not endorsements, predictions, or characterizations of any candidate. Forecaster race ratings are deliberately excluded: they are third-party predictions, not ballot facts.
_meta.rating_note: Race ratings are third-party forecaster labels (Cook Political Report, Decision Desk HQ, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball, Silver Bulletin) describing expected competitiveness. They are predictions, not ballot facts and not results.

Governor Greg Abbott did not call a special election to fill the remainder of the term, so unlike the 18th district in 2025-26 there is no separate special-election contest on this ballot: the November 3 general election is the only U.S. House race here, and the winner is not seated until the new Congress convenes in January 2027, leaving the district unrepresented in the interim. Three candidates appear on the ballot, including the state's only qualified independent U.S. House candidate. Reported by the Texas Tribune in October 2026 as one of the state's competitive U.S. House races.

sourcing_flags: 23 - Field itself is firmly confirmed by three sources (Herrera R, Padilla Stout D, Mendoza I). Flagged because the ballot structure is unusual and was widely misreported: although Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned effective April 14, 2026, Governor Abbott never called a special election for the remainder of the term, so there is NO special election alongside the regular race. Earlier reporting and the companion reps.json anticipated one. Confirmed by Wikipedia, Texas Public Radio, Houston Chronicle and the absence of any CD 23 special election in The Green Papers' Texas 2026 calendar (which does list the CD 18 special).

1 - Field (Moran R, Prince D) confirmed by three sources. Flagged because Wikipedia's general-election results table for this district also lists an independent, 'Sonia Canciola' (spelled 'Sonia Canchola' elsewhere in the same article, itself an unresolved inconsistency). No independent qualified for the ballot in District 1: the SOS independent-filing page lists Ben Mendoza (District 23) as the only certified independent U.S. House candidate statewide, and the only District 1 declaration of intent on the SOS tracking list was filed by Nathan Levin Jackson. Canchola/Canciola is EXCLUDED from the field above.

27 - Field (Cloud R, Lloyd D) confirmed by three sources. Flagged because Wikipedia's general-election results table also lists 'Dan McQueen (Independent)', former mayor of Corpus Christi. No independent qualified in District 27. The SOS declaration-of-intent list shows two different McQueens who filed and did not qualify: Eldon Daniel McQueen (District 21, Comal County, engineer) and Travis Daniel McQueen (District 27, Nueces County, contractor); Wikipedia separately lists 'Eldon Dan McQueen, former mayor of Corpus Christi' under District 21, conflating at least two people. McQueen is EXCLUDED from the field above. Separately, Wayne Raasch is a certified write-in here and so is not printed on the ballot.

30 - Field (Haynes III D, Jackson R) confirmed by five sources (Tribune/AP SOS data, The Green Papers, Wikipedia, KERA, CBS Texas, Fox 4). Flagged only because it CONFLICTS WITH THE COMPANION FILE: reps.json lists 'Venton Jones' as the District 30 Democratic nominee. That appears to be an error in reps.json; Venton Jones does not appear in any source as a candidate in this primary. reps.json was not modified.

33 - Field (Allred D, Gillespie R) confirmed by three sources. Flagged for two labeling hazards: (a) Colin Allred is a FORMER member of Congress, not the incumbent, and the prior version of this file incorrectly marked him incumbent; (b) Michelle Craig is a certified write-in and is not printed on the ballot.

37 - Field (Casar D, Pena R) confirmed by three sources. Flagged because incumbency is genuinely ambiguous and sources disagree: Wikipedia labels Greg Casar '(incumbent)' because he is a sitting member of Congress, while the SOS/AP ballot data and The Green Papers treat the 37th as an open seat whose incumbent is the retiring Lloyd Doggett, with Casar noted as the incumbent of the old 35th. This file records incumbent: false with an explanatory note. Choose a display convention deliberately.

12 - Field confirmed by three sources, but the Democratic nominee's name form varies: 'Heli Rodriguez Prilliman' (SOS/AP ballot data, used here), 'Angela "Heli" Rodriguez Prilliman' (The Green Papers), 'Angela Rodriguez Prilliman' (Wikipedia). Same person; no conflict about the candidacy.

7 - Field confirmed by three sources, but the Green candidate's name order varies: 'Espoir Ngabo' (SOS/AP ballot data and The Green Papers, used here) versus 'Ngabo Espoir' (Wikipedia's results table, which contradicts the candidate bullet in the same article). Given name is Espoir.

2, 22, 32 - Fields are firmly confirmed; flagged only because the prior single-source version of this file incorrectly marked Steve Toth (2), Trever Nehls (22) and Jace Yarbrough (32) as incumbents. None is an incumbent: Toth is a state representative who defeated incumbent Dan Crenshaw in the primary, Trever Nehls is the retiring incumbent's twin brother, and Yarbrough is running for an open seat whose former incumbent was a Democrat drawn into another district.

NOT FLAGGED, for the record - minor-party ballot qualification was verified rather than assumed. Seven minor-party candidates qualified: Green in districts 7, 28, 31, 34 and 38; Libertarian in districts 26 and 34. Wikipedia additionally lists convention candidates who do not appear in the SOS-derived certified field (for example John E. Foddrill, Libertarian, district 28) and many 'filed paperwork' independents in districts 5, 9, 18, 20, 21, 23, 30, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 37 and 38 who did not qualify; a federal FEC filing or a declaration of intent is not Texas ballot access. None of these are included above.

Cross-check that passed - the number of incumbents on the ballot reconciles with The Green Papers' independent tally of the 119th Congress delegation: 17 Republicans and 8 Democrats renominated. Of those 25, 24 are running in the district they currently represent (marked incumbent: true here) and one, Greg Casar, is running in a different district number (district 37).

A note on the 'five targeted seats' framing - sources differ on which five Democratic-held seats the 2025 map targeted, so no district's race_note asserts membership in a 'five seats' list. Wikipedia and Roll Call frame it by displaced incumbent: the districts of Marc Veasey (old 33rd), Julie Johnson (old 32nd), Al Green (old 9th), Vicente Gonzalez (34th) and Lloyd Doggett (old 37th). The Texas Tribune's October 2026 competitiveness reporting instead names new-map districts 28, 34 and 35 as targeted Democratic seats. The companion reps.json uses a third list (9, 28, 33, 34, 35). These are different framings of the same redraw rather than factual contradictions, but the counts are not interchangeable.
30: one secondary source also lists an independent, Oxford Nordberg, on this ballot; the SOS certified-independent list used here does not. Shown without him pending confirmation.
